The Story of Somsharma Muni

I bow to Lord Jinendra, who teaches the supreme dharma, and I write the story of Somsharma Muni.

Through confession, censure, self-condemnation, vows, fasting, praise, and stories, one should destroy negligence and carelessness — just as the force of poison is destroyed through mantras and medicines. This story is related to this.

In the land of Bharat, in the Pundrak region, in the chief city of Devi Kotpur, there lived a Brahmin named Somsharma. Somsharma was a good scholar of the Vedas and Vedangas — grammar, etymology, prosody, astrology, phonetics, and arts. His wife was Somilya. They had two sons, Agnibhuti and Vayubhuti.

In the same city lived another Brahmin named Vishnudatt, whose wife was Vishnushri. Vishnudatt was wealthy but not good-natured. One day, in some urgent need, Somsharma borrowed some money from Vishnudatt. He could not repay the debt when one day, through a Jain monk's discourse on dharma, Somsharma became detached and took initiation as a monk. From there, wandering and teaching dharma in other cities and villages, he came back to Kotpur once again.

Vishnudatt saw him and caught him, saying, "Holy one, your two sons are now in a state of extreme poverty. They don't have even a single coin. They cannot pay my money. Therefore, either you pay me my money, or sell your dharma."

A very difficult problem arose before Somsharma Muni. He could not think of what to do. Then his guru, Veer-Bhadra Acharya, told him, "Very well, go and sell your dharma!" Following his guru's order, Somsharma Muni went to the cremation ground and began selling dharma. At that time, a goddess came and asked him, "Monk, what is this dharma that you are selling?"

The monk replied, "My dharma is endowed with twenty-eight root virtues and eighty-four lakh secondary virtues. It is of ten types — supreme forgiveness, gentleness, honesty, truth, purity, restraint, austerity, renunciation, non-possession, and celibacy. This is the nature of dharma as declared by Lord Jinendra."

Hearing the monk's explanation of the dharma he was selling, the goddess was greatly pleased. She bowed to the monk and praised dharma, saying, "Monk, what you have said is very true. Dharma is indeed supreme. I shall buy it from you." She gave him the money and took the dharma. Thus Somsharma was freed from his debt, and the goddess, through practising the dharma she had bought, attained liberation.

This story teaches that dharma is the supreme treasure, more valuable than all the wealth in the world. Even when faced with the impossible choice of paying a debt or giving up dharma, the monk found that dharma itself provided the solution. The wise should understand that dharma is never lost when given away — it only multiplies and brings benefit to all.
